headline: weak
texts: Several core areas need rebuilding, and that is a clear starting point. Work through the review cards in the order listed, beginning with the traps you fell into confidently. Do the mechanism and signs first, because later management and imaging build on them. Then retake the module.
Gap: 'most common' is not holding. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Review the opening card before anything else.
Shaky: you know both causes but some age matches slipped. Link each to lymphoid tissue, which atrophies with age.

Gap: the causal chain is not yet reliable. Obstruction comes first; periumbilical visceral pain shifts to the right iliac fossa when the peritoneum is involved, and the end artery explains rapid gangrene. Review the pathophysiology cards.
Gap: symptom order is not yet a tool. Pain first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting first argues against appendicitis. Review the symptom order card.

Gap: the signs and positions are mixed up. Psoas is hip extension with retrocaecal; obturator is internal rotation of the flexed hip with pelvic; Rovsing is left iliac fossa pressure. Start with the sign contrast card.
Gap: Alvarado is not secure. Two items score 2 (RIF tenderness, leucocytosis), the rest 1, total 10; 7 or more is likely. Rebuild it from the table and practise the arithmetic card.
Gap: the imaging ladder is not secure. Ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, MRI if inconclusive in pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Review the imaging cards by patient group.

Gap: pregnancy testing and look-alikes are not yet automatic. Beta-hCG comes first in women of reproductive age; each group has mimics, such as mittelschmerz or caecal carcinoma. Review the differential card.

Gap: the choice between operating and antibiotics-first is not secure. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is for selected uncomplicated adults. Review the management qualifiers card.

Gap: mass, abscess and interval surgery are mixed up. A mass is conservative, an abscess drained under imaging, and older patients need colonoscopy or CT before selective interval surgery. Redo the management ladder cards.

Gap: the complication lists are merged. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection, faecal fistula, stump appendicitis, ilioinguinal injury. Rebuild both lists and review the nerve card.
Gap: the tumour and its size rule are not yet held. Carcinoid is commonest; under 2 cm appendicectomy usually suffices, larger needs right hemicolectomy. Review the tumour card.

You treated psoas and obturator as one 'right hip' idea and assigned the names by feel. Psoas is pain on hip extension; obturator is pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip. Revisit the side-by-side contrast card and recite each by its movement, not its name.

You memorised sign and position as pairs without asking what the appendix touches, so the pairs landed on the wrong position. Retrocaecal lies on the psoas; pelvic lies against rectum, bladder and obturator internus. Redraw the appendix behind and below the caecum, then do the position card again.

You ran Rovsing's sign backwards, putting the pressure where the pain is. The sign is pressure in the left iliac fossa causing right iliac fossa pain. Narrate it aloud as 'press here, hurts there', then revisit the sign contrast card.

You read the disease backwards from its end-point, putting localised right iliac fossa pain or ischaemia first. The true chain starts with obstruction and pressure; early visceral T10 pain is periumbilical and only shifts when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed. Re-do the mechanism segment, saying each step aloud in order.

You stored the symptoms as an unordered list, so vomiting felt like an opening symptom. In appendicitis pain comes first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting before pain argues against it. Review the order card and use pain-first to screen vignettes for gastroenteritis.

You weighted Alvarado items by how specific they feel, not by the table, or read the score as a test result. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2; every other item scores 1, total 10, and 7 or more means likely. Rebuild the score from the table and redo the arithmetic card.

You treated the first-line test as the final word, so a negative or inconclusive ultrasound ended your work-up. In adults, contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test and follows an unhelpful scan. Add CECT to your adult imaging ladder and revisit the imaging card.

You ranked tests by accuracy alone and put MRI first in pregnancy. The first rung is the cheap, safe, available test, graded-compression ultrasound; MRI without gadolinium is the second rung. Redo the pregnancy pathway ordering and keep 'USG, then MRI' as one phrase.

You treated a remembered past-paper key as the current standard and defaulted to ultrasound for adults. Older keys expected ultrasound; current practice uses CECT as the most accurate test in adults. Learn the pair 'USG first, CECT most accurate' and revisit the exam-traps card on it.

You read 'most common' as 'most dangerous' or 'most tested' and picked another emergency. Perforated ulcer or cholecystitis may be graver, but appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, in pregnancy too. Underline the qualifier word and review the opening card.

You treated the classic pattern as the only pattern, so RIF pain meant appendicitis. Each group has its mimics: mesenteric lymphadenitis in children, mittelschmerz and PID in women, caecal carcinoma in the elderly. Make a three-look-alikes list per group and revisit the differential card.

You first gave the cause for the wrong age group, then corrected. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults. Tie it to lymphoid tissue that atrophies with age.

You took 'treatment of choice' as 'only treatment', an absolute older keys used. Appendicectomy remains the treatment of choice, but current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-confirmed uncomplicated adults. Add that to your notes and revisit the treatment contrast card.

You kept 'antibiotics-first is acceptable' and dropped its conditions. It applies to selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease; an appendicolith or complicated disease points to surgery. Review the three qualifiers on the management card, then redo the patient-comparison question.

You treated the old key as fixed policy and applied interval appendicectomy routinely, skipping the malignancy check. Now it is selective, and patients over about 40 need colonoscopy or CT for caecal carcinoma. Revisit the interval-surgery card and add the older-patient work-up.

You read 'appendicitis means operate now' and skipped the first step. A stable mass is managed conservatively by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen, stopped if the pulse, pain or mass worsens; an abscess is drained percutaneously. Re-learn the step order on the management card.

You applied the adult CT answer to every patient and dropped the age and pregnancy qualifier. Ultrasound is first in children and pregnant women; contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults. Ask 'who is the patient?' first and review the three-group imaging contrast card.

You followed the working diagnosis and treated the pregnancy test as an afterthought. In any woman of reproductive age, beta-hCG comes before imaging or theatre, because ectopic pregnancy changes the plan. Re-do the women's step-order card and say 'test pregnancy first'.

You merged the two complication lists from the same chapter and never asked whether each arises from the disease or the operation. Pylephlebitis, mass and abscess are disease; wound infection, faecal fistula and stump appendicitis follow surgery. Rebuild both lists on paper and redo the which-is-not card.

You learned the iliac-region nerves as a bundle and picked a neighbour of the nerve at risk. The gridiron incision endangers the ilioinguinal nerve, causing a right inguinal hernia. Sketch the three neighbouring nerves across the gridiron site and review the nerve card.
You tend to pair items correctly in form but attach them to the wrong partner. Rebuild the pair from the anatomy it depends on rather than recalling the pair.
You tend to run a sequence or direction backwards, starting from the end picture. Narrate the process cause first, 'press here, hurts there' or 'blockage, then pressure'.
You tend to start with the favoured diagnosis and skip the step that comes first. Ask 'what first, and why' before committing to a plan.
You tend to treat the first or most accurate test as the whole pathway. Think in rungs: what comes first, what comes after an unhelpful result.
You tend to drop the qualifier, such as age, pregnancy or appendicolith, and apply a general answer. Circle the patient detail before looking at the options.
You tend to answer from a remembered past-paper key without checking current practice. In such stems, give the old key and the modern view as a pair.
You tend to read a qualifier or a pattern too narrowly: 'most common' as 'most serious', or a classic picture as the only one. Underline the qualifier, then ask what else fits.

You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those are the costly ones, because you stop checking. Before tapping Sure, name the qualifier or the rule you are relying on; if you cannot, tap Guessing.

You used no hints and still fell into traps. Hints on the questions you were unsure about would have flagged the qualifier. Next time, open one before a stem with an age, a pregnancy or an exam-key flavour.

Review the cards in the order shown: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky. Do two or three per sitting, answer before reading, then retake this module in about a week to see which models have changed.
